exp.0:0:
This verse opens the book of Jonah. It says that God spoke to Jonah, who was the son of Amittai. The phrase "the word of the Lord came" means that God gave him a direct message. "Lord" is the name of God, and here the verse only presents the moment when God begins to speak.

This is the start of the story. The one speaking is God, and he addresses Jonah, a prophet. A prophet was someone who received messages from God to deliver to others. A book of kings mentions a prophet named Jonah, son of Amittai, and many believe he is the same man, though the text does not explain this. What follows shows why God speaks to him: he has a mission for him.

God still speaks to people, above all through his Word. Before deciding whether or not we will obey, it is worth pausing to listen carefully. Today we can ask God to speak to us as we read the Bible, and be willing to do what he shows us.
exp.0:2:
This verse tells how Jonah, instead of obeying God, got up and fled. He went down to the port city of Joppa, found a ship headed for Tarshish, paid his fare, and got on board to get away from the Lord's presence. The fare was the cost of the trip. The ship is what he boarded to get away.

God had told Jonah to go to Nineveh, a great city, and announce that its wickedness had come up before Him. The narrator tells us Jonah did the complete opposite. Tarshish lay in the opposite direction, probably far to the west, though its exact location is not known for certain. The text does not explain here why he fled; later in the book, Jonah gives his reason.

When God asks us to do something hard, it is tempting to run away instead of obeying. But no one escapes God. Today we can speak to Him honestly about our fears and ask Him for the courage to do what He asks.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that when the storm came, the sailors became frightened. Each one was calling out to his own god. They also threw the cargo of the ship into the sea to make it lighter. Meanwhile, Jonah had gone down into the inner part of the ship and had fallen asleep.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jonah had disobeyed God and was fleeing in the opposite direction from Nineveh. The sailors, who did not know the God of Israel, did what they knew to do: pray to their gods and try to save the ship. The contrast is strong: the pagans cry out, and the prophet sleeps.

For today: when we drift away from God, we can become drowsy, without noticing the danger around us. Let us ask Him to awaken our hearts, and return to Him sincerely, without waiting for the storm to force us.
exp.0:10:
The sailors ask Jonah what they should do with him so that the sea will calm down. They say this with urgency, because the storm was growing worse. The sea was getting rougher and more violent.

The sailors speak here as men who did not worship the LORD, yet they already knew that Jonah was running away from the LORD. When they hear that he fears the God who made the sea, they are filled with fear and ask him for a solution. Notice that although they did not know God, they treat Jonah with respect and do not act with violence. They seek his counsel before deciding.

For today: when our decisions bring consequences that affect others, the best thing is to acknowledge the truth with humility. God can use even our mistakes to show his power and lead others to respect him.
exp.0:11:
Jonah asks the sailors to pick him up and throw him into the sea. He says that this way the sea will become calm, because he knows the great storm has come upon them because of him.

The speaker is Jonah, the prophet who was running away from God instead of going to Nineveh as God had commanded him. The frightened sailors ask him what they should do. Jonah admits his disobedience and accepts the consequences, even if they cost him his life. The sailors first try to row back to land, and then they pray to God.

For today: when we honestly admit our mistakes, without excuses or blaming others, we open the door for God to work. Taking responsibility also protects those around us from having to bear the consequences of our decisions.
exp.0:12:
The men rowed hard to bring the ship back to land, but they could not succeed. The phrase about bringing the ship back to land means returning the boat to dry ground. The sea was growing more violent and rough.

Jonah had fled from God, and that is why the storm came. He himself told them to throw him into the sea. The sailors, who were not part of God's people, were not quick to do it. They preferred to save Jonah as well. The text does not say exactly why they hesitated, but their desire not to cause a death is evident.

For today: sometimes we want to fix things with our own effort, even though God may be calling us to surrender and obey. If there is something God asks you to face, do not keep rowing against the storm. Confess it and hand it over to Him.
exp.1:7:
He says that Jonah felt he no longer had strength, that his life was fading away. Then he remembered God and prayed.

It is Jonah speaking, the prophet who fled from the mission God had given him. He was thrown into the sea and a great fish swallowed him. From that dark place he cries out to God. This verse marks the moment when, with no way out, he turns his heart back toward the Lord, and God hears him.

Today, when you feel weak or far from God, do not wait until you are better. Remember Him and pray just as you are. God hears even from our darkest places.
exp.2:3:
Jonah begins to walk into the city of Nineveh, going ahead about a day's journey. As he walks, he calls out his message aloud: in forty days, Nineveh will be overthrown.

Dios had sent Jonah to this great city, the capital of a people known for their violence. The narrator tells that Jonah obeyed, though he had earlier run away. The message is brief and does not mention forgiveness, but the people's response shows they understood that there was still a chance to turn back. Some scholars see in this a warning that opens a door to mercy.

For today: God can use a simple, sincere message to touch hearts. Do not wait until you have everything perfect before speaking the truth with love; obey what God places on your heart, and leave the results in his hands.
exp.2:4:
This verse says that the people of Nineveh believed what God warned them through Jonah. As a sign of repentance, they proclaimed a fast, that is, going without food for a time, and they put on sackcloth, a rough cloth that was used to show sorrow. They did this, all of them, from the most important to the most humble. Believing God means they trusted his word. Proclaiming means they announced it out loud.

Here the narrator tells of the reaction to Jonah's preaching. He had announced that in forty days the city would be destroyed. Nineveh was a great city, and the message reached the king, who also humbled himself.

For today: when the Word of God confronts us, it is not enough to hear it. We can respond with humility, acknowledge our failures, and change course, no matter our position or age.
exp.2:5:
The message reached the king of Nineveh. When he heard it, he rose from his throne, took off his royal robe, put on sackcloth (a rough cloth worn as a sign of grief and repentance), and sat down in ashes.

The narrator tells what happened after Jonah announced that Nineveh would be destroyed in forty days. First the people believed, and then the king set the example. His action shows humility before God. The Bible does not say with certainty which king it was, and scholars do not agree on that.

For today: when God speaks to us through his word, the best response is humility. We can set aside pride, acknowledge our failures, and change course, no matter how much power or prestige we have.
exp.2:7:
This verse says that everyone in Nineveh, both people and animals, were to be dressed in sackcloth, which was a rough cloth used as a sign of grief and repentance. They were also to pray to God earnestly and leave their wicked conduct. The word "violence" in the verse means taking what belongs to others by force or theft.

Here the king of Nineveh speaks, along with his nobles. Jonah had announced that the city would be destroyed. The king listened, humbled himself, and ordered a general fast. Including the animals shows how serious the situation was. They did not know whether God would forgive them, but they had hope.

For today: true repentance does not stay in words or gestures of sadness, but changes behavior. Today you can ask God to show you a habit or an unfair way of treating others that you need to leave behind, and take a concrete step to correct it.
exp.3:1:
Jonah prays to God, but he does it with complaint. He reminds God that this is why he fled to Tarshish: he knew that God is gracious (compassionate), good and full of kindness (full of goodness), patient (slow to anger), and abounding in mercy. He also says that God relents from evil, that is, that God can choose not to send the punishment he announced when people change.

Jonah, the prophet, is the one speaking. The people of Nineveh had repented, and God forgave them. Jonah was angry because he did not want that city to receive mercy. His description of God is true, but he uses it harshly, not with gratitude.

For today: it is easy to celebrate God's mercy toward us and to resent it when it reaches those we consider unworthy. Let us ask God for a heart that rejoices when he forgives others, as he rejoiced with you.
exp.3:2:
Jonah asks God to take his life. He says that it is better for him to die than to keep living. It is a sincere prayer, but it is full of anger and discouragement.

The speaker is Jonah, the prophet. God has just spared Nineveh, the enemy city of Israel, because its people repented after his message. Jonah is angry because he knows the character of God, who is merciful and compassionate, and he did not want that people to be forgiven. That is why he had fled to Tarshish. God does not punish him, but calmly asks him whether he is right to be so angry.

When we are upset or discouraged, we can speak to God with complete honesty, as Jonah did. But we should also listen to his questions with humility and ask him to heal our hearts and teach us to have compassion for others.
exp.3:4:
Jonah goes out from Nineveh and settles on the east side of the city. There he builds a shelter, a simple hut of branches, and sits in its shade. He wants to see what will happen to the city.

The narrator of the book is speaking. Jonah is angry because God spared Nineveh when its people repented. God had just asked him whether he was right to be so angry, and Jonah does not answer with words but with his actions. The text does not say clearly what he was expecting: perhaps that God would still punish the city, but the passage does not make this clear.

Many times we find ourselves waiting for things to turn out the way we think they should, even when God has already spoken or acted with mercy. Today we can ask ourselves whether our anger is justified or whether we struggle to accept God's compassion toward others. It is good to pray and let God correct our hearts.
exp.3:5:
God prepared a gourd plant (or a vine; the Hebrew word is unclear and is translated in various ways) to grow up over Jonah. Its shade protects him from the heat and relieves him of his discomfort and anger. Jonah becomes very glad because of the plant.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jonah is angry because God spared Nineveh. He sat down to wait outside the city. God gives him this shade as an act of care, and He will soon use it to teach him about His compassion for others.

For today: It is easy to rejoice in what benefits us and forget those whom God also loves. Today you can thank God for His small kindnesses and ask Him for a more compassionate heart toward others.
exp.3:8:
God asks Jonah whether it is right for him to be so angry about the plant that gave him shade and then withered. Jonah answers without hesitation: his anger is so great that he would rather die.

God speaks, and Jonah replies. Jonah was upset because God spared Nineveh when the city repented. God uses the plant as a lesson: Jonah grieves over a plant he did not make grow, yet God has compassion on thousands of people. The book ends with that open question.

For today: examine why you get angry. Sometimes our comfort or our preferences hurt us more than the people God loves. Ask him for a heart with his same compassion.
exp.1:1:
This verse says that Jonah prayed to God, whom he calls "the LORD," while he was inside the fish. The reference to "the belly" is the inside of the fish. Jonah does not stay silent or give up: he speaks with God in the middle of his situation.

The one speaking here is the narrator, who tells what the prophet Jonah did. Earlier, Jonah had fled from the mission God gave him, and that is why he ended up in the sea. God prepared a great fish that swallowed him, and he stayed there three days and three nights. The verses that follow show the content of his prayer: he cries out in his distress and acknowledges that God heard him.

For today: even if we have made mistakes or feel we are in a dark place, we can pray with sincerity. God is not far from anyone who calls on Him with humility.
exp.2:2:
So Jonah got up and went to Nineveh, in accordance with the word of the LORD. This time he did not run away. The text describes Nineveh as an exceedingly great city, requiring a three-day journey.

The narrator tells us that God spoke to Jonah a second time, after Jonah had tried to escape. Nineveh was an important city of Assyria. It is not known for certain whether the three-day journey refers to its size, to the time needed to walk through it with his message, or to both; scholars interpret it in different ways.

God is able to give us another chance when we fail. If there is something He asked you to do that you have put off, do not wait until you feel perfect: get up and take the first step of obedience today, even if the task seems enormous.
exp.0:1:
God gives Jonah an order: "Get up! Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before Me." The word "preach" here means to proclaim a message publicly, and the phrase about the wickedness coming up before God means that God has seen that wickedness and does not ignore it.

The Lord speaks, and his message is for Jonah, a prophet, son of Amittai. Nineveh was an important city of Assyria, a powerful nation that was not Israel. God gives Jonah a mission of warning. The next verse shows that Jonah did not want to obey and tried to flee in the opposite direction. The text does not explain his reason here; the book makes it clear later.

For today: God cares about justice and also about people who may seem distant or hard to love. Ask him to show you whom he wants you to speak his truth to, and obey with courage even when it costs you.
exp.2:8:
Here the king of Nineveh asks: "Who knows? God may turn and relent, and turn from his fierce anger, so that we will not perish." The word "relent" here speaks of God changing his decision, not of his having done something wrong.

The king and his nobles speak after Jonah announced that the city would be destroyed. They believed the message, fasted, put on sackcloth, and gave up violence. They make no demands of God; they only hope that he will have mercy. The following verse shows that God saw their change and did not send the punishment.

For today: when we know that we have failed, we can come to God with humility and without excuses, leaving behind what is truly wrong. We do not deserve his forgiveness, but we can trust that he is compassionate.
exp.3:0:
This verse says that Jonah was deeply upset and greatly displeased. The phrase "he became angry" means he felt a heavy weight in his heart, a deep bitterness, and that his reaction was strong, not a passing annoyance.

The narrator tells us what Jonah felt. He had just preached in Nineveh, and the city repented, so God did not destroy it. Jonah was angry about this. His prayer that follows explains that he knew God's mercy and did not want it extended to Nineveh, an enemy of his people. Some understand that he also felt hurt at being seen as a false prophet, although the text emphasizes above all his complaint against God's compassion.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we rejoice when God shows mercy to those who seem undeserving to us. Let us bring our anger honestly to God, as Jonah did, and ask him for a heart like his.
exp.1:4:
Jonah 2:5 is part of the prayer Jonah offers from inside the great fish. He describes how the waters closed in on him: "The waters engulfed me to take my life; the watery depths closed around me; the seaweed wrapped around my head." The verse shows how close to death he felt.

This is Jonah speaking, the prophet who ran away from the task God had given him. After being thrown into the sea, he prays from the belly of the fish. He feels distant from God because of his disobedience and the danger he is in. The verse itself does not say more about his longing, so we should not read too much into it.

For today: when you feel that your mistakes or your problems have pulled you away from God, do not stay silent. Like Jonah, pray honestly and hold on to the hope of drawing close to Him again.
exp.3:3:
God asks Jonah a question: "Have you any right to be angry?" He does not rebuke him harshly, but invites him to consider whether his anger is justified. The word "angry" means being very upset or deeply irritated.

Jonah had preached in Nineveh, and the city repented. God had compassion and did not destroy it. Jonah became angry, and in his prayer he admits that he fled to Tarshish because he knew that God is gracious and merciful. God responds with patience, seeking to have Jonah examine his heart.

Today, when we become angry because God forgives someone we believe does not deserve it, this question serves us. Before we react, we can stop and ask ourselves honestly: does my anger reflect the heart of God, or only my pride? God corrects us with love and teaches us to have compassion.
exp.1:8:
This verse says that those who cling to "empty things," meaning worthless things that promise help but cannot give it, such as idols or false securities, turn away from "mercy," which here means God's faithful love. The phrase "they forsake their own mercy" can be understood as meaning they abandon God, who is the source of their mercy.

Jonah speaks from inside the fish. He has just been rescued from death after he prayed to God. Now he contrasts his experience with that of those who trust in empty things. Next he promises to offer sacrifice to God with a voice of thanksgiving and to fulfill what he has vowed. He ends with the declaration: "Salvation is from the LORD!"

For today: ask yourself where you place your trust when everything gets complicated, whether in money, success, or the opinion of others. Those things can disappoint. Return to God in prayer, because his mercy remains available.
exp.0:8:
Here Jonah answers the sailors' questions. He says that he is a Hebrew, that is, an Israelite, and that he worships the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land. Here "worship" means revering and honoring God.

The sailors were fleeing a terrible storm. They cast lots to learn who was to blame, and the lot fell on Jonah. Then they asked him who he was. Jonah answers with a statement of faith, although his conduct contradicts his words, since he was running away from God. The irony is that he says God made the sea, right where he was fleeing.

Our words of faith must go hand in hand with our obedience. If we say that we honor God, let us ask Him for help to live as we say, and let us return to Him with humility when we have gone astray.
exp.3:6:
God sent a worm at dawn the next day. The worm attacked the gourd plant, and the plant dried up. The gourd was the plant that had been giving Jonah shade. Some believe it was a vine with large leaves, though no one knows for certain what kind of plant it was. Here the phrase "attacked the plant" means that the worm struck it, and "withered" means that it dried up.

This is part of the end of the book. Jonah is angry because God spared Nineveh when its people repented. The narrator tells how God uses the plant, the worm, and the wind to teach Jonah about compassion. What Jonah felt for the plant prepares the way for God's question about Nineveh.

For today: sometimes we grieve our lost comforts more than the people who are in need. Let us ask God for a compassionate heart, one that cares for others as much as it cares for what is its own.
exp.1:0:
Here the word "prepared" means ready or arranged in advance. God provided a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah spent three days and three nights inside it. The text does not say what kind of fish it was.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. Jonah had run away from God's command to go to Nineveh and ended up thrown into the sea during a storm. This fish does not appear as a mere punishment; it is the means God uses to keep him alive. Right after, in the next verse, Jonah prays from there.

For today: even when we have made bad decisions, God does not abandon us. You can pray from wherever you are, with sincerity, and trust that he knows how to rescue you.
exp.2:1:
God speaks to Jonah a second time and tells him to get up and go to Nineveh, "the great city." There Jonah is to proclaim a message to the people, a public announcement. God says he will give Jonah the message, and Jonah will not make it up himself.

God speaks. Earlier, Jonah had run away in the opposite direction and ended up in the belly of a great fish. Now God gives him another chance. Nineveh was an enormous city, and the book shows that God cares about peoples beyond Israel. Why Jonah hesitated at first is explained later in the book.

God knows how to give us second chances. If you have failed at something God asked of you, you can return to Him, listen with humility, and obey. What matters is passing on what God says, not what we would prefer to say.
exp.0:7:
The sailors, after the lot pointed to Jonah, ask him a string of questions one after another. They want to know who is to blame for the calamity that has come upon them, and they also want to know who he is: what his work is, where he has come from, what his country is and who his people are. "Occupation" means work or trade. The "calamity" they mention is the danger of the storm.

The sailors speak with fear and desperation. They had cast lots to discover who was responsible, and the lot fell on Jonah. Before they act, they want to understand everything about him. Their answer in the following verse will reveal that Jonah was fleeing from God.

For today: when things become difficult, God can use honest questions to make us look at who we are and to whom we belong. It is good to answer with sincerity, without hiding the truth, and to be willing to acknowledge our mistakes.
exp.3:10:
God asks Jonah whether he should not care about Nineveh, a great city with more than 120,000 people who cannot tell their right hand from their left. This phrase is usually understood to mean people who cannot tell good from evil, or who live without guidance; some think it refers to young children. The verse also mentions the many animals in the city. "Care" here means mercy and tender concern.

God speaks, and the book ends with this open question. Jonah had become angry because God spared Nineveh, and also because of the plant that withered. God uses that plant to show him that if Jonah grieved over a plant, then all the more God grieves over people.

For today: examine your heart. Is there someone you consider unworthy of forgiveness? Ask God to give you his compassion for that person, and pray for them.
exp.1:6:
Jonah says he went down to the deepest part of the sea, where the mountains have their roots. He feels that the earth closed around him like the bars of a prison, with no way out, and that he would be shut in forever. But then he turns and says "but you": God brought his life up out of the pit, a word that here means the deep pit or the grave. "The Lord" is the name of God.

Jonah speaks here, the prophet who ran away from the task God gave him. Thrown into the sea, he was swallowed by a great fish and prayed from there. That is why he uses poetic language: he felt as if he were already dead. Now he acknowledges that God rescued him.

For today: when you feel there is no way out, do not stay fixed on what seems to be forever. Cry out to God with sincerity, even if you have gone wrong. He can lift your life up from the darkest place.
exp.0:13:
The sailors call out to the LORD, the God of Jonah. They plead, "Please, O LORD," which means they are begging him. They ask not to die because of Jonah's life, and that God not hold them guilty of innocent blood, that is, of killing a man who does not deserve it. They admit that the LORD does as he pleases.

These sailors are not Israelites. They had called on their own gods before this storm. Jonah had been running from the LORD and told them the storm had come because of him. They tried to row back to land but could not make it. Now, fearful of doing something unjust, they ask the LORD to spare them before they throw Jonah into the sea.

For today: when you face a hard decision, pray before you act. Acknowledge that God governs all things, and ask him for wisdom and forgiveness. He lets himself be found by anyone who seeks him with humility.
exp.1:3:
Jonah says that God cast him down into the deep, into the heart of the sea. The current surrounded him, and the waves and billows passed over him, covering him completely.

Jonah speaks from the belly of the fish. He had disobeyed God and fled on a ship, and was thrown into the sea during a storm. Although the sailors cast him overboard, he acknowledges that God was directing everything. His prayer speaks of distress, but it already shows that he cries out to God and trusts that God hears him.

For today: when we go through moments that seem about to drown us, even because of our own mistakes, we can call on God with sincerity. He continues to hear, and discipline does not always mean abandonment.
exp.1:2:
He says that Jonah asked God for help in his distress and that God heard him. The phrase "belly of the grave" is a poetic way of saying "from the realm of the dead," which in the Hebrew is "Sheol." "Heard" means "listened."

It is Jonah speaking, the prophet who fled from the mission God had given him. He fell into the sea and a great fish swallowed him. From there he prayed. This verse opens his prayer, and it begins by recalling that God had already answered him. Some understand that he is speaking of his complete rescue; others, that he is speaking of the confidence with which he prays even from inside the fish.

For today: even if you have failed or feel you are in a dark place, you can speak with God honestly. He does not turn away from anyone who cries out to Him. Pray today, without embellishment, and tell Him what is troubling you.
exp.0:16:
Now the LORD had appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish. The word "appointed" means that God arranged or sent the fish at that moment. The text says "great fish" without specifying what kind of animal it was.

The narrator of the book tells what happened after the sailors threw Jonah into the sea. He had fled from God, who had sent him to preach in Nineveh. When he fell into the water, the storm calmed. This verse shows that God did not abandon Jonah, even though he was disobedient. The fish was a rescue and also an opportunity to return to God.

For today: when you make mistakes or drift away, do not think that God has let you go. He can use even your darkest moments to call you back again. Speak to Him honestly and return to Him.
exp.2:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Jonah a second time. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time" means that a message from God came to him again. The word "then" ties this moment to what came before, and the colon introduces what God is about to tell him to do right away.

The one speaking is God, and He is speaking to Jonah, a prophet. Earlier, Jonah had fled from the task of going to Nineveh, and he ended up in the sea and inside a great fish. Now God does not set him aside, but repeats the assignment to him. The verses that follow show that Jonah obeys and goes to Nineveh, a very large city.

For today: even if you have failed or drifted away, God can offer you another opportunity. If He speaks to you again, respond with humility and obedience, and take today that step you know He is asking of you.
exp.0:14:
This verse says that the sailors, after trying everything, picked up Jonah and threw him into the sea. Immediately, the raging sea grew calm. A note on wording: "the raging sea grew calm" means the sea stopped its violent churning and became still.

The narrator tells what happened on the ship. Jonah was running from God, and he himself had told them to throw him into the sea. The sailors did not want to do it: they rowed hard, and then they prayed to the LORD, asking that they not be held responsible for the death of an innocent man. When they saw the calm, they feared God and offered sacrifice to him.

For today: when our decisions cause problems, the best thing is to acknowledge the truth and face it with humility. And notice the sailors: in the face of difficulty, they cried out to God, and He is sovereign over all things, even over the storms.
exp.3:9:
God speaks to Jonah and reminds him of what happened with the plant, a leafy vine that gave him shade. The words "you cared about the plant" mean that Jonah felt sorry for it. God points out that Jonah did not tend it or make it grow; it sprang up in a night and perished in a night.

The Lord speaks. Jonah was angry because God had spared Nineveh when its people turned from their wrongdoing. God made the plant grow and then made it wither, to teach him something. Jonah grieved over a plant, but not over thousands of people. The next verse completes the lesson: God does have compassion on Nineveh.

Today we might ask ourselves whether our own comforts matter to us more than people do. Let us ask God for a heart like his, one that has compassion even on those we find hard to love, and let us pray for them.
exp.0:9:
The sailors were filled with even greater fear once they learned who Jonah's God was. They asked him, "What have you done?" because they understood that he was running away from the presence of the LORD, since he himself had told them so. The verse is that "even more afraid" means their fear had grown, and "the LORD" refers to the God of Israel.

These are non-Israelite sailors, frightened by the storm. Jonah had just told them that he was a Hebrew and that he worshiped the God who made the sea and the land. They understood that running away from that God was a serious mistake. Their question sounds like both a rebuke and amazement.

Running away from God never frees us from Him or from the consequences, and it can also affect others. Today we can stop, recognize the ways we have avoided obeying Him, and return to Him sincerely, knowing that God welcomes those who repent.
exp.0:15:
This verse says that the sailors felt deep reverence and awe toward the LORD, the God of Israel. The phrase "feared the LORD greatly" does not speak only of fright, but of recognizing his power. That is why they offered a sacrifice to him and made vows to him, that is, they made solemn promises to serve him or give him thanks.

The one telling the story is the author of the book. The sailors were men from different nations who worshiped their own gods. Jonah was fleeing from God, and a storm nearly sank the ship. When they threw him into the sea, the storm calmed at once. They saw that the LORD had power over nature. The text does not say in detail what vows they made.

For today: when God shows you his care in the middle of a crisis, respond with gratitude and sincere devotion, not only with relief. Take a moment to give him thanks and to renew your commitment to him.
exp.0:6:
This verse tells how the sailors, in the middle of a violent storm, decided to cast lots to find out who was responsible for the calamity. Casting lots was like drawing straws or picking a marked stone or token to settle a question. The lot fell on Jonah.

The ones speaking are the sailors, frightened because they had already called on their gods and thrown the cargo into the sea without any relief. They believed the storm had a spiritual cause. Jonah was running from God's command to go to Nineveh, and he was sleeping below deck. The Bible does not explain how the lot worked, but here God uses it to point to Jonah.

For today: when trouble comes, it is wise to stop and humbly ask God whether there is something we should acknowledge or correct, instead of blaming others or continuing to run away.
exp.3:7:
He says that as the sun was rising, God appointed a scorching east wind. The sun beat down on Jonah's head so that he grew faint and wished to die. He said it was better for him to die than to live.

The narrator tells what happened after Jonah sat outside Nineveh, angry because God had spared the city. God provided a plant to give Jonah shade, and then sent a worm that withered it. Through the wind and the sun, God prepares a lesson for Jonah about his hard heart and God's compassion.

When something takes away our comfort, it is easy to become angry and think only of ourselves. Today we can ask: does my comfort matter to me more than the people God loves? Let us ask for a more compassionate heart, like God's.
exp.0:3:
It says that God hurled a great wind upon the sea, and such a violent storm arose that the ship was in danger of breaking apart. The name of God appears in the text as LORD, and the sea is referred to in a form that was common in older writing. The phrase about the ship means that people feared the boat would be destroyed.

Here the narrator of the book of Jonah speaks. God had asked the prophet to go to Nineveh, but Jonah fled in the opposite direction, toward Tarshish. The storm is no accident: the text says that the LORD sent it. It shows that Jonah could not escape from God, and also that God was seeking to get the prophet's attention, even for the sake of the sailors.

For today: when we try to run away from what God asks of us, he does not abandon us. Sometimes difficulties invite us to stop, to be honest, and to listen to him again. Today you might ask him: "Lord, is there something I am avoiding?"
exp.2:6:
This verse tells us that in Nineveh an official order was given, in the name of the king and his nobles. Neither people nor animals were to eat or drink, whether herd or flock. The word "proclaimed" means announcing something aloud in public, and the order says no one or no animal was to eat or drink anything at all.

The account shows us the king of Nineveh and his leading men responding to Jonah's message. The people had already believed God and fasted, and the king made that response apply to the whole city. Including the animals was a sign of humility and urgency. The text says no more, so it is best not to claim details it does not state.

For today: when God shows us something wrong in our lives, let us not put it off until later. We can respond with sincere humility, acknowledge what we have done, and change direction, starting today.
exp.1:5:
Jonah says that he went down to the roots of the mountains, and that the earth itself closed around him and barred him in. The image is of being shut in below the mountains, completely cut off and unable to escape. Those are the words of a man who believed he was beyond rescue.

It is Jonah speaking, the prophet who ran from the mission God had given him. He was thrown into the sea during a storm, and God sent a great fish that swallowed him. From there he prays, acknowledging that he was far from God, yet he still cries out to the LORD, his God, believing that God can raise his life from the pit.

For today: when you feel that troubles surround you and you see no way out, do not stop praying. Jonah cried out to the LORD even from the depths, and God heard him. No situation is too deep for Him to hear you.
exp.1:9:
This verse shows Jonah promising to worship God with songs of thanksgiving. He says he will do what he has vowed, and he admits that salvation comes only from the Lord. Then God commands the fish, and it vomits Jonah onto dry land. The word "vomited" here means the fish threw him up onto the shore, and "the LORD" is the name of God. Keeping a vow means doing what you promised.

Jonah speaks from inside the great fish, after disobeying God and running away. On the brink of death, he remembered the Lord and prayed. His prayer ends with confidence: although his situation seemed hopeless, he believes God can rescue him. Then God acts, and Jonah is set free.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, do not forget to thank Him and to keep what you promised Him. And remember that salvation does not depend on your own strength, but on Him.
exp.2:9:
This verse says that God saw the actions of the people of Nineveh: they had turned away from their evil ways. Then God relented from the disaster he had threatened to bring on them, and he did not carry it out.

The narrator here is the one telling the book of Jonah. God had sent Jonah to warn that Nineveh would be destroyed. The king and the people answered with fasting, sackcloth and prayer. The words that come just before this verse show they had no guarantee, only hope in God's mercy. Some understand that God does not change his character, but responds with justice and compassion to what people do.

For today: if there is something in your life that you know is wrong, do not wait. Return to God sincerely and change your conduct; He receives with mercy anyone who truly turns away from wrongdoing.
exp.0:5:
The captain of the ship went to Jonah and asked him, "How can you sleep? Get up and call on your God. Perhaps this God will consider us, so that we may not perish." He wanted Jonah to get up and pray to his God in the hope that God would show mercy and spare them.

The captain, a pagan man, was desperate because of the storm. Every sailor was already crying out to his own god, but Jonah slept, even though he had fled from the presence of God. It is remarkable that a foreigner calls the prophet to prayer. His uncertainty shows that he did not know God well, yet he did hold hope in God's mercy.

For today: do not fall asleep spiritually when there is crisis around you. Pray for those who are suffering, and let God use even an unexpected voice to wake you.

sum.2: God speaks to Jonah a second time and sends him to Nineveh, and this time he obeys and announces that the city will be destroyed in forty days. The people of Nineveh believe God, fast, dress in sackcloth, and turn away from their evil ways, from the king down to the least of them. When God sees their change, He relents from the punishment and does not carry it out.
sum.0: God tells Jonah to go to the great city of Nineveh and warn its people about their wickedness. But Jonah runs away, boarding a ship headed in the opposite direction. God sends a violent storm, and Jonah asks the sailors to throw him into the sea to save them. When they do, the sea grows calm, and the sailors fear the LORD and offer sacrifices to him.
sum.1: God sent a large fish that swallowed Jonah, and he stayed there three days and three nights. From that dark place, Jonah prayed. He remembered how God had heard him in his distress and promised to give thanks, because salvation comes from Him. Then God commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land.
sum.3: Jonah became angry because God spared Nineveh, since he knew that God is gracious and merciful. God gave Jonah a leafy plant that provided shade and then withered, and asked him whether it was right for him to be angry. God taught Jonah that He has compassion on Nineveh, with its many thousands of people and animals.
